stem: Researchers studying secondary hypertension in pigs place a clip on the right renal artery, reducing its cross-sectional area to 30% of baseline.  The left renal artery remains widely patent.  Several days later, which of the following changes is most likely to be seen compared to baseline?​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased inferior vena cava aldosterone level

options.label: C
options.text: Increased glomerular filtration in the right kidney

options.label: D
options.text: Increased renin production in the left kidney

options.label: E
options.text: Increased sodium excretion in the left kidney

explanation:
This experiment illustrates the effects of unilateral renal artery stenosis, which reduces perfusion pressure in the affected kidney.  The resulting hormonal response raises systemic blood pressure but has different effects on the stenotic and nonstenotic kidneys.

In the stenotic kidney (right kidney), decreased perfusion pressure stimulates renin secretion by juxtaglomerular cells, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).  Angiotensin II causes systemic arteriolar vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone secretion.  Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the late distal tubule and collecting duct, promoting sodium and water retention.  These effects cause secondary hypertension, which helps support perfusion of the stenotic kidney.

The nonstenotic kidney (left kidney) is exposed to elevated systemic pressure, which suppresses renin secretion (Choice D) and decreases tubular sodium reabsorption.  Consequently, sodium excretion increases despite elevated circulating aldosterone levels, a response termed pressure natriuresis.  The accompanying water excretion limits extracellular volume expansion, but hypertension persists because the stenotic kidney continues to drive RAAS activation.

(Choices A and B)  With renal artery stenosis, RAAS activation increases systemic aldosterone levels (including those measured in the inferior vena cava) and increases systemic vascular resistance through angiotensin II–mediated arteriolar vasoconstriction.

(Choice C)  Reduced perfusion pressure tends to decrease glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in the stenotic kidney.  Angiotensin II preferentially constricts efferent arterioles, helping preserve glomerular capillary pressure and GFR; however, an increase in GFR above baseline is not expected.  A compensatory increase in filtration by the nonstenotic kidney can help maintain normal overall GFR and serum creatinine despite reduced filtration by the stenotic kidney.

Educational objective:Unilateral renal artery stenosis activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing systemic vasoconstriction and sodium retention that raise blood pressure and help support perfusion of the stenotic kidney.  Increased perfusion pressure in the nonstenotic kidney suppresses renin secretion and promotes sodium excretion (pressure natriuresis), limiting extracellular volume expansion.​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌
